decks.title: The Theory of the Firm — Part 1: Revenue and Producer’s Equilibrium
goals: State the features of perfect competition and explain why a firm is a price taker
Compute total, average and marginal revenue and draw their curves
State the two conditions of producer’s equilibrium
Find the profit-maximising output and the profit from a cost schedule

slides.heading: A Firm in a Perfectly Competitive Market
slides.body_md: Part 1: **revenue** concepts and the firm’s **equilibrium** output.

visual.alt: Route map of part 1: perfect competition, price taker, revenue concepts, producer’s equilibrium
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: In this part we study a firm that sells in a market with very many sellers. We find out why such a firm cannot choose its price, see how its revenue behaves, and learn how it decides the output that gives the largest profit.

slides.heading: Features of perfect competition
slides.body_md: A **perfectly competitive market** has many buyers and sellers, an identical product, free entry and exit and perfect knowledge.

rows: Large number of buyers and sellers
Each seller supplies a very small share of the market
No single seller can influence the price
Every seller’s product is identical in the eyes of buyers
A seller cannot charge more than the others
Firms can join or leave the market without barriers
Above-normal profit attracts entry; losses drive firms out
Buyers and sellers know the price and the quality
No buyer pays, and no seller accepts, a different price

visual.alt: Table of the four features of perfect competition, with their meaning and their effect on the firm
visual.caption: Features of perfect competition.

slides.narration: Perfect competition has four features. There are a large number of buyers and sellers, so each seller is tiny. The product is homogeneous, meaning identical. Firms may enter or leave freely. Buyers and sellers have perfect knowledge of the price and the quality. Together these features give the market a single price.

slides.heading: The firm is a price taker
slides.body_md: A **price taker** accepts the price fixed by the market and can sell any quantity at it.

nodes.label: Many buyers and sellers, identical product
Market demand and supply fix one price
The firm accepts it: a price taker
It can sell any quantity at that price

visual.alt: Flow showing how the features of perfect competition lead to a price taker that can sell any quantity at the market price
visual.caption: Why the firm is a price taker

slides.narration: In such a market, demand and supply of all buyers and sellers together fix one price. A single wheat farm supplies a tiny share, so it cannot change that price. If it asked for more, buyers would go elsewhere. If it asked for less, it would lose money. It therefore takes the price as given.

slides.heading: Total, average and marginal revenue
slides.body_md: **TR = p × q**, **AR = TR ÷ q** and **MR = ΔTR ÷ Δq**.

rows: All the money received from selling q units at price p
Revenue per unit sold; equals the price
Addition to total revenue from selling one more unit

visual.alt: Table defining total revenue, average revenue and marginal revenue with their formulas
visual.caption: Revenue concepts.

slides.narration: Total revenue is the price multiplied by the quantity sold. Average revenue is total revenue divided by the quantity, so it is revenue per unit. Marginal revenue is the change in total revenue when one more unit is sold. We now compute all three for an imagined wheat farm.

slides.heading: Sukhdev’s wheat farm: the revenue schedule
slides.body_md: The market price is Rs 2,000 a quintal. Total revenue rises by the same amount for each quintal.

visual.alt: Table of the imagined revenue of Sukhdev's wheat farm at 2000 rupees a quintal: total revenue 2000, 4000, 6000, 8000, 10000, 12000, average revenue and marginal revenue 2000 at every quantity
visual.caption: Imagined wheat farm, Ratanpur, price Rs 2000.

slides.narration: Sukhdev’s imagined farm in Ratanpur sells wheat at 2000 rupees a quintal. With one quintal total revenue is 2000, with four it is 8000, and with six it is 12000. Average revenue and marginal revenue are 2000 at every quantity.

slides.heading: Total revenue curve
slides.body_md: TR is a **straight line from the origin**; its slope is the price, so a higher price gives a steeper line.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: revenue of an onion plot
slides.body_md: Kamla’s onion plot sells at Rs 18 a kilogram. Find TR, AR and MR.

rows: MR of the 4th ten kg (per kg)

visual.alt: Worked table for Kamla's onion plot at 18 rupees a kilogram: total revenue of 30 kg 540, average revenue 18, marginal revenue 18 per kilogram
visual.caption: Imagined onion plot.

slides.narration: The imagined onion plot sells at 18 rupees a kilogram. For thirty kilograms total revenue is 18 times thirty, which is 540. Dividing by thirty gives average revenue of 18. Selling ten more kilograms raises revenue by 180, so marginal revenue is 18 per kilogram. All three equal the price.

slides.heading: Quick check: total revenue
slides.body_md: Compute the total revenue from 4 quintals.
slides.narration: Multiply the market price by the number of quintals sold. Do not add the cost, and remember that the price is the same for every quintal. Give your answer in rupees.

slides.heading: AR and MR are one horizontal line
slides.body_md: **AR = MR = price** at every quantity, so the curve is a horizontal line at the market price.

slides.narration: Average revenue is the price. Marginal revenue is also the price, because every extra quintal is sold at the same price. The two curves therefore lie on top of each other as one horizontal line at 2000 rupees. If the market price rises to 2500, the line moves up.

slides.heading: Why AR equals MR
slides.body_md: A constant price means each extra unit adds exactly the price to total revenue.

nodes.label: Price stays the same at every quantity
Each extra unit adds the price to total revenue

visual.alt: Flow from a constant price to marginal revenue and average revenue both equal to the price
visual.caption: Why AR = MR = price

slides.narration: The reason is simple. The firm sells every unit at one price. So the extra revenue from one more unit is that price, which is marginal revenue. The revenue per unit is also that price, which is average revenue. For a price taker the two cannot differ.

slides.heading: Quick check: revenue and price
slides.body_md: True or false: marginal revenue of an onion plot is lower than its average revenue.
slides.narration: Think about what happens to the price when the plot sells more. For a price taker the price is the same at every quantity. Compare the extra revenue from one more kilogram with the average revenue per kilogram, then decide whether the statement is true or false.

slides.heading: Profit and the equilibrium conditions
slides.body_md: **Profit = TR − TC.** A producer is in equilibrium where **MR = MC** and **MC is rising**.

nodes.label: Find the output where marginal cost equals the price
Check that marginal cost is rising there
Profit is total revenue minus total cost

visual.alt: Flow of the steps to find a profit-maximising output and the profit
visual.caption: Producer’s equilibrium

slides.narration: Profit is total revenue minus total cost. A firm in perfect competition has marginal revenue equal to the price. It increases output as long as the extra unit adds more to revenue than to cost. It stops where marginal revenue equals marginal cost, provided that marginal cost is rising at that output.

slides.heading: Diya Candles: the cost schedule
slides.body_md: Diya Candles has a fixed cost of Rs 220 a day. Its marginal cost falls at first and then rises.

visual.alt: Table of the imagined costs of Diya Candles with total fixed cost 220: total variable cost 100, 190, 250, 320, 400, 500, 620, 760, 920, total cost 320, 410, 470, 540, 620, 720, 840, 980, 1140, marginal cost 100, 90, 60, 70, 80, 100, 120, 140, 160
visual.caption: Imagined Diya Candles (Rs per day); total fixed cost 220.

slides.narration: Diya Candles is an imagined candle maker. Its fixed cost is 220 rupees a day. Marginal cost is 100 for the first hundred candles, falls to 60 for the third, and then rises to 160 for the ninth. Average cost is lowest at 120 rupees.

slides.heading: Finding the output at a price of 140
slides.body_md: At price 140, MR = 140. MC reaches 140 at 8 hundred, and profit is largest there.

visual.alt: Table for Diya Candles at a price of 140: marginal revenue 140 equals marginal cost 140 at 8 hundred candles, where profit is 140; the ninth hundred adds 160 to cost, more than the price
visual.caption: Imagined Diya Candles at price Rs 140.

slides.narration: Suppose the price is 140 rupees per hundred candles, so marginal revenue is 140. Marginal cost equals 140 at 8 hundred candles, and it is rising. Profit is 140 rupees there. The ninth hundred would add 160 to cost, more than the price, so profit would fall.

slides.heading: Quick check: shape of AR
slides.body_md: Pick the shape of the average revenue curve.
slides.narration: Average revenue is the price. Ask whether the price changes as the farm sells more. For a price taker it does not. Choose the shape of a curve that stays at the same height.

slides.heading: Why marginal cost must be rising
slides.body_md: At price 90, MC = 90 at 2 hundred but MC is **falling**. Profit is higher further on, at 5 hundred.

visual.alt: Table for Diya Candles at a price of 90: marginal cost equals 90 at 2 hundred candles but is falling there, profit at 2 hundred is -230 and is highest, -170, at 5 hundred where marginal cost is rising
visual.caption: Imagined Diya Candles at price Rs 90.

slides.narration: At a price of 90, marginal cost equals 90 at two hundred candles. But marginal cost is still falling there, so the next candles cost less than the price and add to profit. Profit at two hundred is -230. It is highest, -170, at five hundred, where marginal cost is rising.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: equilibrium at a price of 160
slides.body_md: Find the equilibrium output and profit of Diya Candles at price 160.
bullets: Step 1 — MR = 160; MC = 160 at **9** hundred, and it is rising.

visual.alt: Worked table for Diya Candles at a price of 160: output 9 hundred, total revenue 1440, total cost 1140, profit 300
visual.caption: Imagined Diya Candles.

slides.narration: At a price of 160 rupees, marginal revenue is 160. Marginal cost reaches 160 at 9 hundred candles. Total revenue is 1440. Total cost is the fixed 220 plus variable 920, which is 1140. Profit is the difference, 300 rupees.

slides.heading: The equilibrium diagram
slides.body_md: The AR = MR line cuts the rising MC curve at **E**. The shaded rectangle is profit: (price − AC) × output.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Many buyers and sellers, identical product, free entry and exit, perfect knowledge
Accepts the market price; can sell any quantity at it
TR = p × q (straight line from origin); AR = TR ÷ q = p; MR = ΔTR ÷ Δq = p
MR (= price) = MC, with MC rising

visual.alt: Summary table of part 1: perfect competition, price taker, revenue concepts, profit and the equilibrium conditions

slides.narration: To recap. Perfect competition has many buyers and sellers, an identical product, free entry and exit and perfect knowledge. The firm is a price taker. Its total revenue is a straight line from the origin, and average and marginal revenue equal the price. It maximises profit where marginal revenue equals marginal cost and marginal cost is rising.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: List the **features** and link them to **price taker**.
Write **TR = p × q**, **AR = TR ÷ q**, **MR = ΔTR ÷ Δq** before computing.
Say that **AR = MR = price**: a horizontal line; TR is a straight line from the origin.
State **both** conditions: **MR = MC** and **MC rising**.
Show **Profit = TR − TC** with the figures.
slides.narration: Some tips. List the features of perfect competition and link them to the idea of a price taker. Write the formulas for the three revenue concepts before you compute. Remember that average and marginal revenue equal the price. State both conditions of equilibrium, and show the profit with figures.

decks.title: The Theory of the Firm — Part 2: Supply
goals: Explain the shut-down and break-even prices
Derive the firm’s supply curve from marginal cost
Explain the law of supply, its determinants, and movement versus shift
Add firm supplies to get market supply and compute elasticity of supply

slides.heading: From Costs to Supply
slides.body_md: Part 2: **shut-down**, **break-even**, the **supply curve** and **elasticity of supply**.

visual.alt: Route map of part 2: shut-down and break-even prices, the firm supply curve, the law and determinants of supply, market supply, elasticity of supply
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: This part asks when a firm should keep producing and how much it will supply at each price. We find the shut-down price and the break-even price, build the supply curve of a firm, add firms to get market supply, and measure how strongly supply responds to price.

slides.heading: Short-run decision: produce or shut down
slides.body_md: Compare **price** with the minimum of **AVC**. Below it, close; at or above it, produce where MR = MC.

nodes.label: Is price at least minimum AVC?
No: shut down; loss equals fixed cost
Is price at least minimum AC? Then profit is normal or more

visual.alt: Flow of the short-run decision: compare price with minimum average variable cost, then produce or shut down, and compare with minimum average cost
visual.caption: Short-run decision of a price taker

slides.narration: In the short run fixed cost has to be paid even if nothing is made. So the firm compares two losses. If the price is at least the lowest average variable cost, revenue covers variable cost, and the firm produces where marginal revenue equals marginal cost. If not, it is better to stop.

slides.heading: Shut-down price: Diya Candles
slides.body_md: Minimum AVC is Rs 80. At price 70 producing loses 260, more than the fixed cost 220.

visual.alt: Table of the short-run decision of Diya Candles with fixed cost 220: at price 70 producing loses 260, so it shuts down; at 80 the loss equals the fixed cost; at 100 producing loses only 120, so it produces
visual.caption: Imagined Diya Candles; minimum AVC is 80.

slides.narration: For Diya Candles the lowest average variable cost is 80 rupees. At a price of 70, producing loses 260, which is more than the fixed cost of 220, so the firm stops. At 80 the two losses are equal. At 100, producing loses only 120, so the firm keeps producing.

slides.heading: Break-even price
slides.body_md: Minimum AC is Rs 120. At this price TR = TC and the firm earns **normal profit**.

visual.alt: Table of Diya Candles at prices 100, 120 and 140: profit -120, 0 and 140, with zero profit at the break-even price 120
visual.caption: Imagined Diya Candles.

slides.narration: The break-even price is the lowest average cost, 120 rupees. At this price revenue just equals total cost, so profit is zero. This is normal profit, the minimum reward needed to keep the owner in business. Below it the firm makes a loss, and above it the firm earns more than normal profit.

slides.heading: Shut-down point and break-even point
slides.body_md: MC cuts AVC at its minimum (**shut-down point**) and AC at its minimum (**break-even point**).

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a pottery at two prices
slides.body_md: Karigar Pottery has fixed cost Rs 150. Decide at prices of 70 and 90.
bullets: Step 1 — At 70: MC = 70 at 5 pots; profit = 350 − 420 = **-70**.
Step 2 — AVC at 5 pots = 54, below 70, so the pottery continues.
Step 3 — At 90: 6 pots; profit = 540 − 510 = **30**.

visual.alt: Worked table for Karigar Pottery with fixed cost 150: at price 70 output 5 pots, profit -70, average variable cost 54 below the price so it continues; at 90 output 6, profit 30
visual.caption: Imagined Karigar Pottery.

slides.narration: At a price of 70, the pottery makes 5 pots and loses 70. Its average variable cost is 54, below the price, so it continues, because the loss is less than the fixed cost of 150. At 90, it makes 6 pots and earns a profit of 30.

slides.heading: Quick check: shut-down price
slides.body_md: Find the lowest average variable cost.
slides.narration: Divide each total variable cost by its output to get average variable cost. Then pick the smallest value. That value is the shut-down price. Be careful to use only variable cost, not total cost.

slides.heading: Law of supply
slides.body_md: Other things unchanged, a **rise in price** raises the **quantity supplied**.

nodes.label: Higher marginal cost is now covered

visual.alt: Flow from a rise in price to a higher quantity supplied, the law of supply
visual.caption: Law of supply

slides.narration: The law of supply says that, other things remaining the same, when the price of a good rises the quantity supplied rises, and when it falls the quantity supplied falls. The reason is that a higher price covers the higher marginal cost of extra output, so producing more becomes profitable.

slides.heading: Determinants of supply
slides.body_md: Own price moves the point; **technology, input prices, taxes, related goods and number of firms** shift the curve.

rows: Shifts right: more at each price
Shifts left: cost per unit rises
Shifts left; a subsidy shifts it right
Price of an alternative product rises
Shifts left: resources move to the alternative

visual.alt: Table of determinants of supply: own price gives a movement; technology, input prices, taxes and subsidies, prices of related goods and the number of firms shift the curve
visual.caption: Determinants of supply.

slides.narration: Besides its own price, supply depends on other things. Better technology and cheaper inputs raise supply at every price. A tax on each unit lowers it, and a subsidy raises it. If the price of an alternative product rises, producers move towards it and supply of this good falls. More firms in the market mean more supply.

slides.heading: Quick check: effects on supply
slides.body_md: Match each event with its effect on the supply curve.
slides.narration: For each event, decide whether it changes the cost of producing bricks. A lower cost shifts supply to the right and a higher cost shifts it to the left. A change in the price of the good itself moves the point along the same curve. Match carefully.

slides.heading: Movement along and shift of the curve
slides.body_md: A change in **own price** moves along the curve; a change in **another determinant** shifts the whole curve.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: more firms and a tax
slides.body_md: Find market supply at price 8000 with a fourth kiln and with a tax of Rs 1,000.
bullets: Step 1 — Three kilns: 8 + 6 + 6 = **20** thousand bricks.
Step 2 — A fourth kiln adds 6: 20 + 6 = **26**, a rightward shift.
Step 3 — With a tax of Rs 1,000 sellers behave as at 7000: **13**, a leftward shift.

rows: Tax of Rs 1,000 on three kilns

visual.alt: Worked table at 8000 rupees: three kilns supply 20, with a fourth kiln 26, and after a tax of 1,000 rupees 13 thousand bricks
visual.caption: Imagined kilns of Dhanpur.

slides.narration: At eight thousand rupees the three kilns supply 20 thousand bricks. A fourth kiln of the same kind as Bhoomi adds 6, giving 26, so the curve shifts right. A tax of one thousand rupees means sellers keep only seven thousand of the price, so they supply 13, and the curve shifts left.

slides.heading: Price elasticity of supply
slides.body_md: **es = % change in quantity supplied ÷ % change in price.**

visual.alt: Flow showing elasticity of supply as the percentage change in quantity supplied divided by the percentage change in price
visual.caption: es = % change in quantity ÷ % change in price

slides.narration: Elasticity of supply tells us how strongly quantity supplied responds to a change in price. It is the percentage change in quantity supplied divided by the percentage change in price. A large value means that quantity is very responsive. A small value means that quantity responds little.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: elasticity of Anand Bricks
slides.body_md: Price rises from 6000 to 8000; Anand supplies 4 then 8 thousand bricks.
bullets: Step 1 — % change in quantity = (8 − 4) ÷ 4 × 100 = **100**.
Step 3 — es = 100 ÷ 33.33 = **3**, greater than one.

visual.alt: Worked table for Anand Bricks between 6000 and 8000 rupees: quantity rises 100 per cent, price rises 33.33 per cent, elasticity of supply 3
visual.caption: Imagined Anand Bricks.

slides.narration: The quantity rises from 4 to 8, which is 100 per cent. The price rises from 6000 to 8000, which is 33.33 per cent. Dividing the first by the second gives an elasticity of supply of 3. Supply is elastic, because quantity changes by a larger percentage than price.

slides.heading: Classes of elasticity of supply
slides.body_md: es is **greater than**, **equal to** or **less than one**; **zero** (vertical) or **infinite** (horizontal).

sections.heading: 1. Perfect competition and the price taker
sections.body_md: A **perfectly competitive market** has a large number of buyers and sellers, a homogeneous product, free entry and exit of firms and perfect knowledge. Because each firm supplies a tiny share and its product is identical to others, the firm cannot influence the market price: it is a **price taker** and can sell any quantity at that price.

key_terms.definition_md: A market with a large number of buyers and sellers, a homogeneous product, free entry and exit and perfect knowledge.
A firm that has to accept the price fixed by the market and cannot change it by its own output.
A product that buyers regard as identical whichever seller supplies it.

rows: Large number of buyers and sellers

A seller cannot charge more than the others
Firms can join or leave the market without barriers
Above-normal profit attracts entry; losses drive firms out
Buyers and sellers know the price and the quality
No buyer pays, and no seller accepts, a different price

sections.heading: 2. Revenue: TR, AR and MR
sections.body_md:
**Total revenue** TR = p × q. **Average revenue** AR = TR ÷ q = p. **Marginal revenue** MR = ΔTR ÷ Δq.

Under perfect competition AR = MR = price, so each is a horizontal line at the market price, and TR is a straight line from the origin whose slope is the price. For the imagined wheat farm at Rs 2000 a quintal, TR for 1 to 4 quintals is 2000, 4000, 6000, 8000.

key_terms.definition_md: The total money received from selling a given quantity: price multiplied by quantity.
Total revenue divided by the quantity sold: revenue per unit, equal to the price.
The change in total revenue when one more unit is sold.

sections.heading: 3. Producer’s equilibrium: MR = MC
sections.body_md:
**Profit = TR − TC.** A firm that wants the largest profit chooses the output at which (1) **MR (= price) = MC** and (2) **MC is rising** (or at least not falling) at that output.

For imagined Diya Candles at a price of Rs 140 per hundred, MC = 140 at 8 hundred candles, TR = 1120, TC = 980 and profit = 140. At a price of Rs 90, MC = 90 also at 2 hundred, but MC is falling there, so the best output is 5 hundred.

key_terms.definition_md: The output at which a firm maximises its profit: marginal revenue equals marginal cost and marginal cost is rising.

sections.heading: 4. Shut-down and break-even
sections.body_md:
**Short run:** the firm produces only if price ≥ the minimum of AVC, the **shut-down price** (Rs 80 for Diya Candles). Below it, revenue does not cover variable cost and the loss is larger than the fixed cost.

**Long run:** the price must be at least the minimum of AC, the **break-even price** (Rs 120), where TR = TC and the firm earns **normal profit**. MC cuts AVC and AC at these minimum points.

key_terms.definition_md: The price equal to the minimum of average variable cost; below it a firm stops producing in the short run.
The price equal to the minimum of average cost, at which total revenue equals total cost.
The minimum reward needed to keep the entrepreneur in the business; it is counted as a cost, so total revenue equals total cost.

sections.heading: 5. The firm’s supply curve and the law of supply
sections.body_md:
The **supply curve of a firm** in the short run is the **rising part of its MC curve above the minimum of AVC**. For Diya Candles the quantities supplied are 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 hundred at prices of 80, 100, 120, 140, 160 rupees, and nothing below 80.

**Law of supply:** other things unchanged, when the price of a good rises, the quantity supplied rises, and falls when the price falls.

key_terms.definition_md: The quantity of a good that producers are willing to offer for sale at each price.
Other things unchanged, the quantity supplied of a good rises when its price rises and falls when its price falls.
A table showing the quantity supplied at each price.

sections.heading: 6. Determinants, movement and shift
sections.body_md:
Supply depends on the good’s **own price**, **technology**, **prices of inputs**, **unit taxes and subsidies**, **prices of related goods** and (for the market) the **number of firms**.

A change in the own price causes a **movement along** the supply curve (expansion or contraction). A change in any other determinant **shifts** the curve: to the right for better technology, cheaper inputs, a subsidy or more firms; to the left for dearer inputs, a tax, or a rise in the price of an alternative product.

key_terms.definition_md: A change in quantity supplied caused only by a change in the price of the good itself.
A change in the quantity supplied at every price, caused by a change in a determinant other than the good’s own price.

rows: Shifts right: more at each price
Shifts left: cost per unit rises
Shifts left; a subsidy shifts it right
Price of an alternative product rises
Shifts left: resources move to the alternative

sections.heading: 7. Market supply and elasticity of supply
sections.body_md:
**Market supply** is the horizontal sum of the supplies of all firms at each price; at Rs 8000 the imagined kilns supply 8 + 6 + 6 = 20 thousand bricks. It also depends on the number of firms.

**Price elasticity of supply** es = (% change in quantity supplied) ÷ (% change in price), found with percentages of the original values. Classes: es > 1 (elastic), es = 1 (unit elastic), es < 1 (inelastic), es = 0 (vertical curve), es infinite (horizontal curve). For Anand Bricks between Rs 6000 and Rs 8000, es = 100 ÷ 33.33 = 3.

key_terms.definition_md: The total quantity all firms together offer at each price: the horizontal sum of the individual supply curves.
The percentage change in quantity supplied divided by the percentage change in price.

- **TR = p × q**, **AR = TR ÷ q = p**, **MR = ΔTR ÷ Δq = p**: AR = MR is a horizontal line, TR a straight line from the origin.
- Equilibrium needs **MR = MC** and **MC rising**; then **Profit = TR − TC**.
- **Shut-down price** = minimum AVC (short run); **break-even price** = minimum AC (normal profit).
- **Firm supply curve** = rising MC above minimum AVC; **market supply** = horizontal sum.
- Separate a **movement** (own price) from a **shift** (other determinants).
- **es** = % change in quantity ÷ % change in price; classify against one; never use the geometric method.

questions.stem_md: Which one of the following is NOT a feature of perfect competition, as seen in the imagined wheat market of Ratanpur?

options.text_md: A large number of buyers and sellers
A few large sellers who can each fix the market price
Free entry into and exit from the market
Homogeneous product sold by every seller

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** A few large sellers who can each fix the market price. In perfect competition no single seller is big enough to move the price, so the price is fixed by the market as a whole. The other three options are features: many buyers and sellers, a homogeneous product, and free entry and exit.

questions.stem_md: Sukhdev sells wheat in the Ratanpur market at the going price and cannot sell more by charging less or sell any at all by charging more. Economists call such a firm

options.text_md: a price maker
a price leader
a price fixer
a price taker

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** a price taker. A firm that must accept the price set by the market is a price taker. A price maker or fixer chooses its own price, and a price leader sets a price that others follow, which needs market power.

questions.stem_md: Because every wheat seller in the Ratanpur market offers grain of the same kind, a seller who asks for more than the going rate

options.text_md: loses all his buyers to other sellers
keeps all his buyers because of his name
gains buyers who prefer the higher price
earns a rise in marginal revenue

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** loses all his buyers to other sellers. With a homogeneous product buyers see no difference between sellers, so they go to someone charging the market price. Brand loyalty needs differences, and a higher price does not attract buyers.

questions.stem_md: On a graph with quantity of wheat sold on the horizontal axis and revenue in rupees on the vertical axis, the total revenue curve of a price-taking firm is

options.text_md: a horizontal straight line
a U-shaped curve
an upward-sloping straight line starting at the origin
a straight line starting on the vertical axis

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** an upward-sloping straight line starting at the origin. Total revenue is price times quantity with the price constant, so it rises by the same amount for each extra unit and is zero when nothing is sold. A horizontal line would describe a fixed cost and a U shape describes a per-unit cost.

questions.stem_md: The average revenue curve of Sukhdev’s wheat farm, drawn with quantity on the horizontal axis, is

options.text_md: a downward-sloping line
an upward-sloping line from the origin
a horizontal line at the market price
a vertical line at the quantity sold

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** a horizontal line at the market price. Average revenue is total revenue divided by quantity, which is the price, and the price is the same at every quantity for a price taker. The other shapes require the price to change with quantity.

questions.stem_md: Total revenue of Sukhdev’s wheat farm rises from Rs 8,000 to Rs 10,000 when it sells a fifth quintal. The marginal revenue of that quintal is

options.text_md: Rs 2,000, which equals the market price
Rs 10,000, which equals total revenue
Rs 2,000, which is below the market price
Rs 1,000, which is half the market price

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Rs 2,000, which equals the market price. Marginal revenue is the change in total revenue: 10000 minus 8000 is 2000, and for a price taker this equals the price. 10000 is the total, and the other figures divide by a wrong number.

questions.stem_md: The price of wheat in Ratanpur rises from Rs 2,000 to Rs 2,500 a quintal. The total revenue curve of Sukhdev’s farm will

options.text_md: become horizontal
remain the same, since quantity is unchanged
become a curve that bends upwards
remain a straight line from the origin but become steeper

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** remain a straight line from the origin but become steeper. The slope of the total revenue line is the price, so a higher price makes it steeper; at 6 quintals total revenue rises from 12000 to 15000. It is still a straight line from the origin because the price is constant at each quantity.

questions.stem_md: Free entry and exit means that when the imagined brick kilns of Dhanpur are earning more than normal profit, new kilns

options.text_md: cannot enter, which keeps the price high
enter the market, which pushes supply up and the price down
enter the market, which pushes the price up
leave the market, which lowers the number of sellers

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** enter the market, which pushes supply up and the price down. High profit attracts new sellers when entry is free. Their output raises supply and pulls the price down until profit returns to normal. Entry cannot push the price up, and exit takes place when profit is below normal.

questions.stem_md: Besides marginal revenue being equal to marginal cost, a producer maximises profit only if at that output marginal cost is

options.text_md: rising, so that further output costs more than it earns
falling, so that further output costs less than it earns
zero, so that output is free
above average cost

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** rising, so that further output costs more than it earns. If marginal cost were still falling, one more unit would cost less than the price received and add to profit, so output would not be at its best. The second condition is that marginal cost rises, or at least does not fall, at that output.

questions.stem_md: Diya Candles, an imagined candle maker, has marginal cost of 100, 90, 60, 70, 80, 100, 120, 140, 160 for 1 to 9 hundred candles, in rupees per hundred candles. At a market price of Rs 140 per hundred, its profit-maximising output is

options.text_md: 3 hundred candles, where marginal cost is lowest
8 hundred candles, where marginal cost equals 140
7 hundred candles, where average cost is lowest
9 hundred candles, the largest output in the schedule

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** 8 hundred candles, where marginal cost equals 140. Marginal revenue equals the price, 140, and marginal cost reaches 140 at 8 hundred candles on its rising part. Lowest marginal cost and lowest average cost are different points, and the largest output has marginal cost 160, above the price.

questions.stem_md: At a price of Rs 90 per hundred candles, Diya Candles finds that its marginal cost is 90 at 2 hundred candles, where marginal cost is still falling. What should the firm do?

options.text_md: Stay at 2 hundred candles, because marginal revenue equals marginal cost there
Close down, because marginal cost is falling
Expand to 5 hundred candles, because marginal cost is below the price beyond 2 hundred and rises to 80
Stay at 2 hundred candles, because average cost is lowest there

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Expand to 5 hundred candles, because marginal cost is below the price beyond 2 hundred and rises to 80. Equality of marginal revenue and marginal cost is necessary but not sufficient: at 2 hundred the next candles cost less than 90, so profit can still grow. Profit at 2 hundred is Rs -230 against Rs -170 at 5 hundred, where the marginal cost is rising and nearest the price.

questions.stem_md: In the short run a firm in a perfectly competitive market covers its variable cost only if the price is at least

options.text_md: the minimum of its average fixed cost
its total fixed cost
the maximum of its marginal revenue
the minimum of its average variable cost

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** the minimum of its average variable cost. The lowest price at which the firm is willing to produce in the short run is the minimum of its average variable cost, called the shut-down price. Fixed cost is paid whether or not it produces, and average fixed cost has no minimum.

questions.stem_md: The market price of candles falls to Rs 70 per hundred. Marginal cost of Diya Candles equals 70 at 4 hundred candles, but the minimum average variable cost is Rs 80. In the short run the firm should

options.text_md: produce 4 hundred candles, because marginal revenue equals marginal cost
produce where average cost is lowest
raise its price above the market price
produce nothing, since operating loses Rs 260 against Rs 220 if it shuts down

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** produce nothing, since operating loses Rs 260 against Rs 220 if it shuts down. At 4 hundred candles the revenue is 280 and total cost 540, so the loss is 260, larger than the fixed cost of 220 that is lost anyway when production stops. Equality of marginal revenue and cost does not decide when the price is below average variable cost, and a price taker cannot raise its price.

questions.stem_md: From the cost schedule of Diya Candles (total cost of 220, 320, 410, 470, 540, 620, 720, 840, 980, 1140 rupees for 0, 1, 2 … 9 hundred candles), the break-even price per hundred candles, at which the firm just covers all its costs, is

options.text_md: Rs 80, the lowest value of average variable cost
Rs 60, the lowest value of marginal cost
Rs 120, the lowest value of average cost
Rs 126.67, the average cost of the largest output

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Rs 120, the lowest value of average cost. The break-even price is the minimum of average cost, here 120: at 7 hundred candles revenue 840 equals total cost 840. 80 is the shut-down price, 60 is only the lowest marginal cost and 126.67 is not the minimum.

questions.stem_md: When an imagined candle maker earns normal profit, its total revenue is

options.text_md: less than total variable cost
equal to total cost, including the owner’s minimum reward
greater than total cost
equal to total fixed cost alone

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** equal to total cost, including the owner’s minimum reward. Normal profit is the minimum reward that keeps the owner in the business and is counted as a cost, so earning it means revenue just equals total cost. Revenue above total cost is more than normal profit, and revenue below variable cost means closing down.

questions.stem_md: At a price of Rs 100 per hundred, Diya Candles makes a loss of Rs 120 a day at its best output of 6 hundred candles. In the short run the firm should

options.text_md: keep producing, because the loss is smaller than the fixed cost of Rs 220 it would lose by closing
close down at once, because any loss means failure
close down, because the price is below the break-even price of Rs 120
produce nothing, because the price is below average cost at 6 hundred candles

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** keep producing, because the loss is smaller than the fixed cost of Rs 220 it would lose by closing. The price 100 is above the minimum average variable cost 80, so revenue covers all variable cost and part of the fixed cost. Closing would lose the whole 220, while producing loses only 120. A price below break-even does not force closure in the short run.

questions.stem_md: In the long run, an imagined candle maker whose price stays below the minimum of its average cost will

options.text_md: stay for ever, since fixed cost has to be paid
leave the market, since it cannot cover all its costs
raise price to cover the loss
expand output without limit

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** leave the market, since it cannot cover all its costs. In the long run no cost is fixed, so a firm that cannot cover its average cost makes a loss at every output and exits. A price taker cannot raise the price, and expanding output deepens the loss.

questions.stem_md: In the short run the supply curve of a firm under perfect competition is

options.text_md: its entire marginal cost curve, including the falling part
its average cost curve
its average revenue curve
the rising part of its marginal cost curve above the minimum of average variable cost

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** the rising part of its marginal cost curve above the minimum of average variable cost. At each price the firm supplies the output where marginal cost equals price, provided the price is at least the minimum average variable cost. The falling part of marginal cost is not profit-maximising, and average cost or revenue curves give no output for each price.

questions.stem_md: According to the law of supply, other things remaining the same, when the price of a good rises, the quantity supplied

options.text_md: rises
falls
stays the same
first falls and then stays the same

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** rises. There is a direct relationship between the price of a good and the quantity supplied of it, other things unchanged, because a higher price makes supply more profitable.

questions.stem_md: The price of candles falls from Rs 140 to Rs 120 per hundred, and Diya Candles reduces output from 8 to 7 hundred. This is

options.text_md: a leftward shift of the supply curve
a rightward shift of the supply curve
a movement down along the supply curve, called a contraction of supply
an expansion of supply

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** a movement down along the supply curve, called a contraction of supply. When the good’s own price changes, the firm moves along its existing supply curve. A fall in price gives a contraction. A shift would need a change in some other determinant, such as cost or technology, and an expansion is a rise in quantity.

questions.stem_md: The village panchayat of Dhanpur imposes a tax of Rs 1,000 on each thousand bricks sold. At a price of Rs 8,000 the three kilns would earlier supply 20 thousand bricks. After the tax, the quantity supplied at that price is

options.text_md: 27 thousand bricks, because supply shifts to the right
20 thousand bricks, because the price is unchanged
13 thousand bricks, because supply shifts to the left
zero, because every kiln closes

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** 13 thousand bricks, because supply shifts to the left. Sellers keep only the price less the tax, so at 8000 they behave as at 7000 before the tax and supply 13, so the curve shifts left. 27 is the quantity after a subsidy, and the unchanged price does not keep quantity unchanged.

questions.stem_md: A new furnace design lets the imagined kilns of Dhanpur make more bricks from the same coal. Other things unchanged, the supply curve of bricks

options.text_md: shifts to the right, as more is supplied at each price
shifts to the left, as less is supplied at each price
does not move, since price is unchanged
becomes vertical

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** shifts to the right, as more is supplied at each price. Better technology lowers the cost of each brick, so at each price sellers supply more and the curve shifts right. A leftward shift follows a rise in cost, and the price has not changed so there is no movement along the curve.

questions.stem_md: At Rs 7,000 per thousand bricks, Anand Bricks supplies 6 thousand bricks, Bhoomi Bricks 4 thousand and Chandra Bricks 3 thousand. The market supply at that price is

options.text_md: 4.33 thousand bricks, the average
6 thousand bricks, the largest single supply
72 thousand bricks, the product
13 thousand bricks, the horizontal sum

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** 13 thousand bricks, the horizontal sum. Market supply at a price adds up what every firm supplies at that price: 6 + 4 + 3 = 13. An average, a maximum or a product has no meaning as the total offered by the market.

questions.stem_md: A fourth kiln, Dilip Bricks, enters the Dhanpur market. At Rs 8,000 it supplies 6 thousand bricks, the same as Bhoomi Bricks. Market supply at that price changes from 20 to

options.text_md: 14 thousand bricks, a leftward shift
26 thousand bricks, a rightward shift of market supply
20 thousand bricks, with no shift
6 thousand bricks, because only the new kiln counts

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** 26 thousand bricks, a rightward shift of market supply. Market supply depends on the number of firms. Adding a firm adds its quantity at every price: 20 + 6 = 26, so the curve shifts right. Entry never reduces supply, and the old kilns keep supplying.

questions.stem_md: Anand Bricks raises output from 4 to 8 thousand bricks when the price rises from Rs 6,000 to Rs 8,000 per thousand. Its supply is

options.text_md: elastic, with elasticity of supply 3, greater than one
inelastic, with elasticity of supply 0.33, less than one
unitary elastic, with elasticity of supply 1
perfectly inelastic, with elasticity of supply zero

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** elastic, with elasticity of supply 3, greater than one. Quantity rises by 100 per cent and price by 33.33 per cent, so elasticity is 100 divided by 33.33, which is 3. A value above one means quantity responds more than price. 0.33 inverts the ratio.

questions.stem_md: The number of seats in a small imagined hall of Dhanpur is fixed at 500 whatever the price of a ticket. Its supply curve is a vertical line, and the elasticity of supply is

options.text_md: one
zero
greater than one
infinite

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** zero. A vertical curve means quantity does not change when price changes, so the percentage change in quantity is zero and so is the elasticity. Infinite elasticity belongs to a horizontal curve, and one to a line through the origin.

questions.stem_md: Farmers of Ratanpur can grow wheat or mustard on the same field. If the price of mustard rises sharply, the supply of wheat

options.text_md: increases, shifting the wheat supply curve to the right
does not change, since the price of wheat is the same
decreases, shifting the wheat supply curve to the left
moves along the same curve downwards

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** decreases, shifting the wheat supply curve to the left. A higher price of mustard makes mustard more attractive, so land and effort move out of wheat and less wheat is supplied at each wheat price. The wheat price has not changed, so the response is a shift and not a movement along the curve.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** For a price-taking wheat farm, marginal revenue equals the price.

**Reason (R):** Each additional quintal is sold at the same market price, so total revenue rises by exactly that price.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true and R explains A. Marginal revenue is the rise in total revenue from one more unit, and with an unchanged price this rise is just the price.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The average revenue curve of a price-taking firm is a horizontal line.

**Reason (R):** The total revenue curve of a price-taking firm is a straight line through the origin.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both are true, but R does not explain A. Both facts follow from the same cause, a constant price at every quantity; the straight-line total revenue does not make average revenue horizontal.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A producer is not in equilibrium at an output where marginal revenue equals marginal cost if marginal cost is falling there.

**Reason (R):** Beyond that output a further unit adds more to revenue than to cost.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true and R explains A. With marginal cost still falling, the next unit costs less than the price it earns, so extra output raises profit and the producer has not reached the maximum.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** In the short run a price-taking firm stops production when the price falls below the minimum of its average variable cost.

**Reason (R):** When a firm stops production in the short run, it no longer has to pay its fixed cost.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true and R is false. Fixed cost has to be paid in the short run even at zero output; the firm stops because the price does not cover variable cost, so staying open would add to the loss.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A vertical supply curve has infinite elasticity of supply.

**Reason (R):** On a vertical supply curve the quantity supplied does not change when the price changes.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A is false and R is true. If quantity does not change, the percentage change in quantity is zero, so elasticity is zero. Infinite elasticity belongs to a horizontal supply curve.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A tax of a fixed amount on each unit sold shifts the supply curve of candle makers to the left.

**Reason (R):** The tax adds to the cost of supplying every unit, so less is supplied at each price.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true and R explains A. A unit tax is an added cost, so at any given price sellers keep less and offer fewer units.

questions.stem_md: For Kamla’s onion plot, which sells at Rs 18 a kilogram however much it sells, marginal revenue is lower than average revenue at larger outputs.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** At every quantity the average revenue is 18 and the marginal revenue is 18, so the two are equal throughout. A marginal revenue below average revenue needs a price that falls as more is sold.

questions.stem_md: A rise in the price of candles shifts the supply curve of Diya Candles to the right.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** A change in the good’s own price causes a movement along the supply curve, an expansion of supply. A shift comes from other determinants such as cost, technology, taxes or the number of firms.

questions.stem_md: Marginal revenue is the change in total revenue when one more ___ is sold.
questions.solution_md: Marginal revenue is the addition to total revenue from selling one more unit.

questions.stem_md: A fall in the price of bricks, with everything else unchanged, causes a ___ along the supply curve of the kiln.
questions.solution_md: The change in the good’s own price moves the point along the same curve; here it is a downward movement, a contraction of supply.

questions.stem_md: Match each revenue concept used for Kamla’s onion plot with its definition.

options.text_md: Total revenue
Average revenue
Marginal revenue
Profit

match_right.text_md: Total revenue divided by quantity sold, equal to price
Change in total revenue from selling one more unit

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). Total revenue is price times quantity, average revenue is revenue per unit, marginal revenue is the extra revenue from one more unit, and profit is the gap between revenue and cost.

questions.stem_md: Match each event in the imagined brick market of Dhanpur with its effect on the supply curve of bricks.

options.text_md: A new furnace lowers the cost of making bricks
The price of coal used by the kilns rises
A tax is imposed on each thousand bricks
The price of bricks itself falls

match_right.text_md: Downward movement along the same curve
Leftward shift because a tax is added to cost
Leftward shift because input cost rises

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(q), (b)–(s), (c)–(r), (d)–(p). Cost-lowering technology shifts supply right; a dearer input and a unit tax both raise cost and shift it left; the good’s own price only moves the point along the curve.

questions.stem_md: Arrange the steps by which Diya Candles finds its profit-maximising output from a cost schedule at a given market price.

Compute marginal cost from the total cost schedule

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (d) → (b) → (c) → (a). Marginal revenue is set equal to the price first, marginal cost is computed, the output where they are equal on the rising part is located, and the answer is verified with profit.

questions.stem_md: Sukhdev’s wheat farm in the imagined village of Ratanpur sells wheat at the market price of Rs 2,000 a quintal. Find its total revenue from selling 4 quintals.
questions.solution_md: Total revenue = price × quantity = 2000 × 4 = **Rs 8000**.

questions.stem_md: The total revenue of Sukhdev’s farm is 0, 2000, 4000, 6000, 8000, 10000, 12000 (rupees) for 0, 1, 2 … 6 quintals sold. Find the marginal revenue of the 5th quintal.
questions.solution_md: Marginal revenue = 10000 − 8000 = **Rs 2000**, the same as the price.

questions.stem_md: Kamla’s imagined onion plot earns a total revenue of Rs 540 from selling 30 kg of onions. Find its average revenue per kilogram.
questions.solution_md: Average revenue = total revenue ÷ quantity = 540 ÷ 30 = **Rs 18** per kg, which is the market price.

questions.stem_md: The marginal cost of Diya Candles is 100, 90, 60, 70, 80, 100, 120, 140, 160 for 1 to 9 hundred candles, in rupees per hundred candles. If the market price is Rs 120 per hundred, find the output at which marginal revenue equals marginal cost on the rising part of marginal cost.
questions.solution_md: Marginal revenue = price = 120. Marginal cost is 120 at **7** hundred candles, and it rises afterwards to 140.

questions.stem_md: Diya Candles has a total fixed cost of Rs 220 and total variable cost of 100, 190, 250, 320, 400, 500, 620, 760, 920 for 1 to 9 hundred candles. The price rises to Rs 160 per hundred and the firm produces 9 hundred candles. Find its profit per day.

Diya Candles has a total fixed cost of Rs 220 and total variable cost of 100, 190, 250, 320, 400, 500, 620, 760, 920 for 1 to 9 hundred candles. At a price of Rs 100 per hundred it produces 6 hundred candles. Find its profit; give a loss with a minus sign.
questions.solution_md: Total revenue = 100 × 6 = 600. Total cost = 220 + 500 = 720. Profit = 600 − 720 = **Rs -120**, a loss smaller than the fixed cost.

questions.stem_md: Diya Candles has a total fixed cost of Rs 220 and total variable cost of 100, 190, 250, 320, 400 (rupees) for 1 to 5 hundred candles. Find its shut-down price per hundred candles, taking the lowest average variable cost among these outputs.
questions.solution_md: Average variable cost = 100 ÷ 1, 190 ÷ 2, 250 ÷ 3, 320 ÷ 4, 400 ÷ 5, which is 100, 95, 83.33, 80, 80. The lowest is **Rs 80**, at 4 and 5 hundred candles, and it is the shut-down price.

questions.stem_md: The total cost of Diya Candles is 220, 320, 410, 470, 540, 620, 720, 840, 980, 1140 (rupees) for 0, 1, 2 … 9 hundred candles. Find the break-even price per hundred, the lowest value of average cost, taking outputs from 1 to 9 hundred.
questions.solution_md: Average cost = total cost ÷ output: 320, 205, 156.67, 135, 124, 120, 120, 122.5, 126.67. The lowest value is **Rs 120**, at 6 and 7 hundred candles, the break-even price.

questions.stem_md: Karigar Pottery, an imagined pottery, has a total fixed cost of Rs 150 a day and total variable cost of 60, 110, 150, 200, 270, 360 (rupees) for 1 to 6 pots. The price of a pot is Rs 90. Find its maximum profit per day; the marginal cost of the sixth pot is Rs 90.
questions.solution_md: At price 90 the output where marginal cost equals the price is 6 pots. Revenue = 90 × 6 = 540; total cost = 150 + 360 = 510. Profit = **Rs 30**.

questions.stem_md: At Rs 8,000 per thousand bricks, Anand Bricks supplies 8, Bhoomi Bricks 6 and Chandra Bricks 6 thousand bricks a day. Find the market supply at that price.
questions.solution_md: Market supply = 8 + 6 + 6 = **20** thousand bricks.

questions.stem_md: Anand Bricks supplies 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12 thousand bricks at the prices 5000, 6000, 7000, 8000, 9000, 10000 rupees per thousand bricks. Find its elasticity of supply when the price rises from Rs 6,000 to Rs 8,000.
questions.solution_md: Percentage change in quantity = (8 − 4) ÷ 4 × 100 = 100. Percentage change in price = (8000 − 6000) ÷ 6000 × 100 = 33.33. Elasticity of supply = 100 ÷ 33.33 = **3**.

questions.stem_md: Diya Candles supplies 6 hundred candles at Rs 100 and 7 hundred at Rs 120 per hundred. Find its elasticity of supply between these prices, correct to 2 decimal places.
questions.solution_md: Percentage change in quantity = (7 − 6) ÷ 6 × 100 = 16.67. Percentage change in price = (120 − 100) ÷ 100 × 100 = 20. Elasticity = 16.67 ÷ 20 = **0.83**, so supply is inelastic.

questions.stem_md: State any four features of a perfectly competitive market, taking the wheat market of Ratanpur as an imagined example.
questions.solution_md: Any four features, half a mark each.

answer.model_answer_md: Perfect competition has a large number of buyers and sellers, so no one influences the price. The product is homogeneous. Firms can enter and leave freely. Buyers and sellers have perfect knowledge of the price and the product.

questions.stem_md: Why is a single wheat farm in a perfectly competitive market a price taker? Give two reasons.
questions.solution_md: Small share and identical product.

answer.model_answer_md: The farm sells a tiny share of the market output, so a change in its own output does not change the price. The product is homogeneous, so buyers will not pay more to it than to others. It therefore accepts the market price.

marking_scheme.step: Very small share of the market
Homogeneous product, so no higher price is possible

questions.stem_md: Explain why average revenue and marginal revenue are equal for Kamla’s onion plot, which sells at Rs 18 a kilogram, using the figures for the first 20 kg.
questions.solution_md: AR equals price; MR equals price.

answer.model_answer_md: Revenue is Rs 360 for 20 kg and Rs 180 for 10 kg. Average revenue is 360 ÷ 20 = 18. Each extra kilogram adds the same price, so 180 ÷ 10 = 18, equal to average revenue.

marking_scheme.step: Average revenue computed and equal to price
Marginal revenue computed and equal to average revenue, with reason

questions.stem_md: State the two conditions that must hold at the output where a perfectly competitive firm maximises its profit.
questions.solution_md: MR = MC, with MC rising.

answer.model_answer_md: First, marginal revenue, which equals the price, must be equal to marginal cost. Second, marginal cost must be rising at that output, or at least not falling, so that producing beyond it would add more to cost than to revenue.

marking_scheme.step: Marginal cost rising at that output, with reason

questions.stem_md: What is the shut-down point of Diya Candles in the short run? State the price and say what the firm does below it.
questions.solution_md: Minimum AVC, with consequence.

answer.model_answer_md: The shut-down point is where the price equals the minimum of average variable cost, here Rs 80 per hundred candles. Below this price the revenue cannot even cover variable cost, so the firm stops production in the short run and loses only its fixed cost.

marking_scheme.step: Shut-down price as the minimum average variable cost, with the figure
Firm stops below it, loss limited to fixed cost

questions.stem_md: What is the supply curve of a firm in perfect competition, and why does it start at the shut-down price?
questions.solution_md: MC above minimum AVC.

answer.model_answer_md: The supply curve is the rising part of the marginal cost curve above the minimum of average variable cost. At each price the firm chooses the output where marginal cost equals price, and below the minimum average variable cost it would not produce at all.

marking_scheme.step: Supply curve identified with marginal cost above the minimum of average variable cost
Reason: below that price nothing is supplied

questions.stem_md: State the law of supply and give one reason why a rise in the price of bricks makes the kilns of Dhanpur supply more.
questions.solution_md: Direct relation; profit motive.

answer.model_answer_md: The law of supply says that, other things unchanged, the quantity supplied of a good rises when its price rises. At a higher price, the marginal cost of more bricks is covered, so supplying more raises profit and kilns expand output.

marking_scheme.step: Law stated with the condition other things unchanged
Reason: a higher price covers the higher marginal cost

questions.stem_md: Name any four determinants of the supply of a good other than its own price and say what each does to supply when it changes in the favourable direction.
questions.solution_md: Four determinants with direction.

answer.model_answer_md: Technology: better technology raises supply. Input prices: a fall in input prices raises supply. Unit taxes: a tax lowers supply while a subsidy raises it. Prices of related goods: a rise in the price of a substitute good in production lowers supply.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish a movement along the supply curve of bricks from a shift of the supply curve, with the cause of each.
questions.solution_md: Own price versus other determinants.

answer.model_answer_md: A movement along the curve is caused by a change in the price of the good itself, other things unchanged. A shift of the whole curve is caused by a change in another determinant, such as technology, input prices or a tax, and changes quantity at every price.

questions.stem_md: Sukhdev’s wheat farm sells at Rs 2,000 a quintal. Draw up, in words, its total revenue for 1, 2 and 3 quintals and explain why the total revenue curve is a straight line through the origin.
questions.solution_md: Figures; origin; constant slope equal to price.

answer.model_answer_md: Total revenue is 2000, 4000, 6000 rupees for 1, 2 and 3 quintals. The curve starts at the origin since nothing is earned when nothing is sold. It rises by 2000 for every quintal, as the price is constant, so the slope is constant and the curve is a straight line.

marking_scheme.step: Total revenue figures for 1, 2 and 3 quintals
Constant slope equal to the price

questions.stem_md: Diya Candles has a total fixed cost of Rs 220 and total variable cost of 100, 190, 250, 320, 400, 500, 620, 760, 920 for 1 to 9 hundred candles. Find its profit-maximising output at a price of Rs 140 per hundred and its profit there.
questions.solution_md: MC = price at 8; profit 140.

answer.model_answer_md: Marginal cost is 100, 90, 60, 70, 80, 100, 120, 140, 160 for 1 to 9 hundred candles. It equals 140 at 8 hundred candles, on the rising part. Total revenue is 140 × 8 = 1120, total cost is 980, so profit is 1120 − 980 = Rs 140.

marking_scheme.step: Output where marginal cost equals the price

questions.stem_md: What is the break-even price of a firm? Show from the Diya Candles schedule that at the break-even price its profit is zero.
questions.solution_md: Minimum AC; revenue equals cost.

answer.model_answer_md: The break-even price is the minimum of average cost, where the firm earns just normal profit. For Diya Candles it is Rs 120 per hundred, at 7 hundred candles. Revenue is 120 × 7 = 840, equal to total cost 840, so profit is 0.

marking_scheme.step: Break-even price defined as minimum average cost
Revenue equals total cost, profit zero

questions.stem_md: Anand Bricks supplies 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12 thousand bricks at the prices 5000, 6000, 7000, 8000, 9000, 10000 rupees per thousand bricks. Bhoomi Bricks supplies 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 and Chandra Bricks 0, 0, 3, 6, 9, 12 at the same prices. Find the market supply at Rs 6,000 and at Rs 8,000 and state how it is obtained.
questions.solution_md: 6 and 20 thousand bricks.

answer.model_answer_md: Market supply is the horizontal sum of the supplies of the firms at each price. At 6000 it is 4 + 2 + 0 = 6 thousand bricks. At 8000 it is 8 + 6 + 6 = 20 thousand bricks.

questions.stem_md: Lakshmi Looms, an imagined handloom unit, raises its supply of dupattas from 100 to 120 a week when the price rises from Rs 200 to Rs 240 each. Find its elasticity of supply and say whether supply is elastic, unit elastic or inelastic.
questions.solution_md: es = 1.

answer.model_answer_md: Quantity rises by 20 per cent and price by 20 per cent. Elasticity of supply is the percentage change in quantity divided by the percentage change in price, which is 20 ÷ 20 = 1. As the elasticity equals one, supply is unit elastic: quantity changes by the same percentage as price.

marking_scheme.step: Percentage change in price and ratio

questions.stem_md: A tax of Rs 1,000 per thousand bricks is imposed on the kilns of Dhanpur, whose market supply is 2, 6, 13, 20, 27, 34 thousand bricks at 5000, 6000, 7000, 8000, 9000, 10000 rupees. Find the market supply at Rs 7,000 and Rs 9,000 after the tax and say how the curve moves.
questions.solution_md: 6 and 20, leftward shift.

answer.model_answer_md: At a price p sellers keep p − 1000, so they supply what they supplied at that lower price. At 7000 supply is 6 thousand bricks, and at 9000 it is 20 thousand bricks. Supply falls at each price, so the curve shifts to the left.

questions.stem_md: Explain how the features of perfect competition make a wheat farm a price taker, and show with Sukhdev’s farm, which sells at Rs 2,000 a quintal, that total revenue is a straight line while average revenue and marginal revenue equal the price.
questions.solution_md: Features; TR; AR; MR.

answer.model_answer_md: There are many buyers and sellers, the product is homogeneous and knowledge is perfect, so each farm sells at the market price and is a price taker. Total revenue is price × quantity: 2000, 4000, 6000, 8000 rupees for 1 to 4 quintals, a straight line from the origin. Average revenue is 8000 ÷ 4 = 2000. Marginal revenue is 8000 − 6000 = 2000. Both equal the price, so both are horizontal.

marking_scheme.step: Features leading to a price taker
Total revenue formula and straight line
Marginal revenue computed and equality with price

questions.stem_md: Explain producer’s equilibrium under perfect competition. Using the marginal cost of Diya Candles (100, 90, 60, 70, 80, 100, 120, 140, 160 for 1 to 9 hundred candles), find its equilibrium output and profit at a price of Rs 160 per hundred, with total cost of Rs 1,140 at that output.
questions.solution_md: Conditions; equilibrium output; profit.

answer.model_answer_md: A firm maximises profit where marginal revenue, which equals the price, is equal to marginal cost, and marginal cost is rising. Here marginal revenue is 160. Marginal cost equals 160 at 9 hundred candles, and it is rising. Revenue is 160 × 9 = 1440. Profit is 1440 − 1140 = Rs 300. Below 9 marginal cost is below the price, so more output adds profit.

marking_scheme.step: Condition: marginal revenue equals marginal cost

questions.stem_md: Diya Candles has a total fixed cost of Rs 220, a minimum average variable cost of Rs 80 and a minimum average cost of Rs 120. Explain the shut-down and break-even prices and what the firm does at prices of Rs 70, Rs 100 and Rs 120.
questions.solution_md: Definitions; three prices.

answer.model_answer_md: The shut-down price is the minimum average variable cost; below it the firm stops. At 70 it loses 260 by producing, more than the fixed cost 220, so it stops. The break-even price is the minimum average cost. At 100, between the two prices, it produces 6 hundred and loses 120, less than 220. At 120, the break-even price, revenue equals total cost, so the firm earns zero profit, which is normal profit. Between 80 and 120 a firm produces in the short run but cannot survive in the long run.

marking_scheme.step: Decision at the low price with figures
Decision at the middle price with figures
Zero profit at the break-even price

questions.stem_md: Derive the short-run supply schedule of Diya Candles from its marginal cost (100, 90, 60, 70, 80, 100, 120, 140, 160 for 1 to 9 hundred candles) and minimum average variable cost of Rs 80, for prices of 80, 100, 120, 140, 160 rupees, and describe the shape of the supply curve.
questions.solution_md: Rule; schedule; shape.

answer.model_answer_md: At each price the firm supplies the output where marginal cost equals price, provided the price is at least 80. The supply is 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 hundred candles at 80, 100, 120, 140, 160 rupees. Below 80 it supplies nothing. The supply curve is the rising part of the marginal cost curve above the minimum average variable cost, so it slopes upwards, showing the law of supply.

marking_scheme.step: Rule: marginal cost equals price above the shut-down price
Nothing supplied below the shut-down price

questions.stem_md: Explain how market supply is obtained from firm supply, using the Dhanpur kilns (the three kilns together supply 2, 6, 13, 20, 27, 34 thousand bricks at 5000, 6000, 7000, 8000, 9000, 10000 rupees). Then show how it changes if a fourth kiln with the supply of Bhoomi Bricks enters, and name two other causes of a shift of supply.
questions.solution_md: Summation; entry; other causes.

answer.model_answer_md: Market supply is the horizontal sum of firm supplies at each price. For the three kilns it is 2, 6, 13, 20, 27, 34 thousand bricks at 5000, 6000, 7000, 8000, 9000, 10000 rupees. With the fourth kiln the supply at 8000 rises from 20 to 26, so the curve shifts right, since market supply depends on the number of firms. Other causes are a change in technology and a tax.

questions.stem_md: Define price elasticity of supply and find it for Anand Bricks between Rs 6,000 and Rs 8,000 (quantities 4 and 8 thousand bricks). Name the classes of elasticity of supply by their values.
questions.solution_md: Definition; computation; classes.

answer.model_answer_md: Price elasticity of supply is the percentage change in quantity supplied divided by the percentage change in price. Quantity rises by 100 per cent and price by 33.33 per cent, so it is 3, greater than one. The classes are greater than one (elastic), equal to one (unit elastic), less than one (inelastic), zero (a vertical curve) and infinite (a horizontal curve). Here quantity responds more than price does.
